tideReference.label: Spring tide reference day
tideReference.caution: Slack windows are a planning aid only, not for navigation.

sites.name: SS Thistlegorm
sites.sinkingCause: Bombed by German Heinkel He 111 aircraft
sites.sinkingHistory: Thistlegorm left Glasgow in June 1941 carrying motorcycles, Bedford trucks, rifles and two steam locomotives for the Eighth Army in North Africa. On the night of 5 October she anchored at Sha'ab Ali to wait for a safe passage through the Gulf of Suez. Two Heinkels returning from a search for a troopship spotted her on the morning of 6 October; one bomb struck the aft magazine and the ship went down in minutes. Nine crew were killed, and the cargo holds have stayed almost intact in the 30 metres of water since.
hazards: Penetration of the holds is easy to enter and hard to exit - stay outside unless wreck-trained and line-laid.
Enclosed space with silt; a fin kick can drop visibility to under a metre.
Boat traffic and live-aboard moorings overhead on the shallowest part of the wreck.
Loose locomotive parts and truck bodies shift on the deck.
sites.entryExit: Descend the mooring line to the starboard bow at 16 m and drift aft along the deck. Return to the same line for the ascent; surface away from the propellers and only after the SMB is flying.
sites.boatTraffic: Several live-aboard and day boats tie to the site each morning. Expect divers surfacing on all sides of the wreck and keep 5 m off the mooring lines.
sites.emergencyPlan: Surface and signal the boat with a delayed SMB. Oxygen and a first-aid kit are carried on every boat at this site; the nearest recompression chamber is in Sharm El Sheikh, roughly 40 minutes by fast boat.

sites.name: RMS Rhone
sites.sinkingCause: Hurricane, driven onto Salt Island rocks
sites.sinkingHistory: Rhone was a fast iron-hulled mail packet on the Southampton to Rio run, and was lying at anchor in Great Harbour when a hurricane's second half arrived on 29 October 1867. Her captain ran for open water but the storm drove her onto the rocks off Salt Island. Cold seawater reached the still-firing boilers and she blew apart, taking 123 of the 145 people aboard with her. She has lain in two pieces since, the stern in 6 to 12 metres and the bow in deeper water.
hazards: The bow section lies in 20 to 26 m - deeper than the stern and past open-water depth limits.
Surge around Salt Island rocks makes the swim between the two sections tiring.
Loose swim-throughs at the bow have silted and narrowed.
Anchoring is prohibited; use the park moorings.
sites.entryExit: Enter from the park mooring over the stern at 6 m and swim forward. Shore-side surge can push you onto the rocks; hold a compass heading back to the mooring and ascend with an SMB.
sites.boatTraffic: National park day boats and charter yachts moor here through the morning. Ferries pass between Salt and Peter Island, so do not drift north.
sites.emergencyPlan: Delayed SMB to the surface, oxygen on the boat, and the call is to the US Virgin Islands search and rescue on VHF 16. The nearest chamber is on St Thomas.

sites.name: USS Spiegel Grove
sites.sinkingCause: Deliberately scuttled as an artificial reef
sites.sinkingHistory: Spiegel Grove served as a dock landing ship for three decades before the reserve fleet and, latterly, the Florida Keys reef programme took her over. She was prepared and sunk on 17 June 2002, though she went down bow first and landed upside down, leaving her stern standing proud of the sand. Hurricane Dennis rolled her upright again in 2005. She is now one of the largest artificial reefs in the Florida Keys and a genuinely demanding swim for recreational divers.
hazards: Superstructure reaches 18 m but the sand is at 40 m - easy to overstay a no-decompression limit.
Strong Gulf Stream current on the outside of the hull.
Overhead penetration through vehicle decks requires wreck certification and a line.
Ladder wells and hatches have sharp metal edges.
sites.entryExit: Descend the mooring line to the superstructure at 18 m, work the deck, and return up the same line. Ascend the mooring rather than drifting, as current can carry you off the site.
sites.boatTraffic: Multiple dive boats and spearfishing charters use the mooring field. Surface close to the buoy and watch for props.
sites.emergencyPlan: Delayed SMB and a shore call to the US Coast Guard on VHF 16. Oxygen is standard on Keys charter boats; the nearest chamber is in Miami.

sites.name: SS Yongala
sites.sinkingCause: Caught by a cyclone, presumed foundered
sites.sinkingHistory: Yongala left Mackay for Cairns on 23 March 1911 carrying 122 passengers and crew and sailed straight into a cyclone that had already wrecked several coastal vessels. She was seen passing Dent Island and then never reported again; the wreck was not found until 1958. All those aboard were lost. The hull now sits almost intact and upright in 30 metres, standing clear of the sand and crowded with marine life.
hazards: Site sits in open water with strong currents and can only be dived at slack.
Occasional bull sharks and the resident giant grouper - keep clear of the wreck floor.
Penetration is closed; the interior is unsafe and unlit.
Moorings are limited and the site is frequently closed after a fatality.
sites.entryExit: Enter from the mooring line on the stern port quarter at 16 m, move along the hull in the lee of the current, and ascend the line with an SMB ready. Missing the mooring means a drift in open water.
sites.boatTraffic: Only permit holders may moor and a maximum of two or three boats visit at once. The site is remote from shipping lanes but the current can carry divers away from the buoy fast.
sites.emergencyPlan: Delayed SMB, oxygen on the day boat, and a VHF 16 call to Townsville Coast Guard. The nearest recompression chamber is in Townsville, four hours by boat.

sites.name: MS Zenobia
sites.sinkingCause: Ballast computer failure during an uncompleted delivery
sites.sinkingHistory: Zenobia was a brand new Swedish ferry on her delivery voyage to Athens when she put into Larnaca to take on cargo. Her automatic ballast control failed, she took on a heavy list and was abandoned on 2 June 1980. She stayed afloat at anchor for five days before sinking on 7 June, and went down with her cargo of trucks and trailers still chained to the decks. She lies on her port side at 42 metres, making her one of Europe's classic deep recreational wrecks.
hazards: Deep and frequently low-visibility: 42 m on sand with a strong thermocline.
Inside the vehicle decks a diver can easily lose buoyancy control in the dark.
Penetration routes are extensive and confusing - line and light are mandatory.
Local fishing gear snags the shallow-starboard structure.
sites.entryExit: Descend the mooring line to the starboard rail at 16 m and work along the hull to the propeller at 40 m before turning the dive. Return to the buoy line for a staged ascent and a full safety stop.
sites.boatTraffic: Day boats from Larnaca moor on the buoy, while local fishing boats cross the bay above the wreck. Keep a delayed SMB up for the whole ascent.
sites.emergencyPlan: VHF 16 to Larnaca harbour control, oxygen and a first-aid kit aboard, and a hyperbaric chamber at Larnaca General Hospital about 20 minutes away.

sites.name: MS Mikhail Lermontov
sites.sinkingCause: Grounded on rocks in Cape Jackson narrows
sites.sinkingHistory: The Soviet liner was on the last leg of a New Zealand cruise when her pilot took her through the narrow passage off Cape Jackson and put her on the rocks on 16 February 1986. She was taken back out into deeper water and deliberately beached, and the 743 people aboard were taken off safely with only one fatality. She went down an hour later and now lies on her starboard side between 12 and 33 metres in a sheltered inlet.
hazards: The wreck is a protected historic site - no penetration except through licensed operators.
Silt and fine sediment inside the promenade decks; visibility collapses in minutes.
Sheltered water hides cold temperatures: 12 to 14 degrees at depth even in summer.
Loose deck fittings and glass in the public rooms.
sites.entryExit: Descend the mooring to the port hull at 12 m and follow the superstructure down to the sand at 33 m before returning up the same line. There is no current swell inside the sound, so a drifting lost line is survivable - but surface close to the buoy.
sites.boatTraffic: Only one vessel at a time is permitted on the mooring, and the sound is otherwise quiet. Ferry traffic passes outside the headland, not over the wreck.
sites.emergencyPlan: Delayed SMB, VHF 16 to Picton harbour radio, oxygen on board. The nearest chamber is at Wellington Hospital, flown from Picton.

checklist.text: Both divers' certification, depth limits and recent dive count confirmed for this site.
Dive plan agreed: maximum depth, turnaround pressure, dive time and who leads the ascent.
Forecast, sea state and the slack window checked against the boat's schedule.
Buddy check: BCD, weights, releases, air on, hoses routed and no dangling straps.
Both divers carry a cutting tool and a torch, and both know where they are stowed.
Surface interval, recall signal and the boat's ladder order briefed to the whole group.
Delayed SMB, reel and whistle accessible; the first diver up knows to release it before ascending.
Emergency plan reconfirmed: oxygen kit location, VHF channel and the nearest recompression chamber.
